issues.subcategory: Table values contradict text description
issues.description: Table 4 reports BFincl values for the follow-up ANOVA on non-illusory errors that directly contradict the text. The text states 'For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42)' and reports 'BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay.' However, Table 4 shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay (strong evidence AGAINST inclusion) and BFincl = 39,110.895 for Target Type (extremely strong evidence FOR inclusion). The text also claims 'the other (non-illusory) error rate was not influenced by target-type (11% for real-letter and pseudo-letter targets),' which is completely inconsistent with a Target Type BFincl of 39,110. Either the table values are from a different analysis, the rows are mislabeled, or the text description is wrong. This undermines confidence in the Experiment 2 follow-up analyses.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42...Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)

issues.subcategory: Direction of effect contradicts reported numbers
issues.description: In Experiment 4, the text states 'There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).' However, 5% is larger than 4%, not smaller. The stated direction of the comparison contradicts the numerical values provided in the same sentence.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.subcategory: High confidence threshold never defined
issues.description: The entire analysis strategy hinges on separating 'high confidence' from 'low confidence' trials, yet the manuscript never explicitly defines which confidence rating(s) (on the 1-4 scale) constitute 'high confidence.' This is critical because the threshold determines both the data that enter the primary analyses and the exclusion of participants (those with too few high confidence trials). Without knowing whether 'high confidence' means ratings of 4, ratings of 3-4, or some other criterion, the analyses cannot be evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty).

issues.subcategory: Very high exclusion rates introducing selection bias
issues.description: Exclusion rates based on insufficient high-confidence trials are very high: 42.5% (17/40) in Experiment 1 and 31.7% (92/290) in Experiment 2. Excluded participants had systematically lower confidence rates (e.g., Exp 1: 26.2% vs 53.8% high confidence trials). This creates a non-random subset of participants who are generally more confident in their responses, which could inflate apparent rates of high-confidence errors and limit generalizability. The characteristics of excluded vs. included participants (beyond confidence rates) are not examined or reported.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric response options inflate pseudo-to-real illusion rate
issues.description: In Experiment 1, on half of pseudo-letter critical trials the pseudo-letter target itself was NOT available as a response option—only its real counterpart was. On these trials, participants who correctly perceived and remembered the pseudo-letter cannot select it and must either choose 'none of these' or select the real counterpart (which would be coded as an illusion). This asymmetry in response availability systematically inflates pseudo-to-real 'illusion' rates relative to real-to-pseudo illusion rates, confounding the world-knowledge interpretation. While acknowledged indirectly and partially addressed in Experiment 2, the Experiment 1 results are still presented as evidence for the main hypotheses.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect timing reported in General Discussion
issues.description: The General Discussion states illusory memories make up almost 20% at '500 ms' for both Experiments 1 and 2. However, in Experiment 1, the Short condition probed memory at 750 ms (0.75 seconds after offset), not 500 ms. Only Experiments 2 and 4 used 500 ms short delays. This misrepresents the temporal characteristics of the Experiment 1 findings.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.subcategory: Incorrect figure reference in Experiment 4
issues.description: The Experiment 4 results section references 'Figure 5' for the error rates, but based on the sequential numbering in the manuscript, the correct figure for Experiment 4 is Figure 6. Figure 5 corresponds to Experiment 3.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: Memory reshaping vs. retrieval difficulty confound
issues.description: The authors infer that the increase in illusory errors over time demonstrates that memory traces are actively 'reshaped' by expectations during STM storage. However, the increase could equally be explained by retrieval-stage processes: as the memory trace weakens, participants may rely more on prior expectations at the point of retrieval, without the stored representation itself being altered. The temporal logic (more illusions at longer delays) cannot distinguish between trace modification during storage and expectation-driven reconstruction at retrieval. This distinction matters for the theoretical interpretation (predictive processing account of storage vs. a simpler retrieval bias account).
issues.quote: correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter

issues.subcategory: High confidence equated with subjective memory experience
issues.description: The authors define 'memory illusions' as high-confidence errors, equating confidence ratings with the phenomenological experience of having an actual (false) memory. However, high confidence on a 4-point scale does not necessarily indicate a vivid, illusion-like memory experience. Participants could be confident for many reasons (e.g., familiarity with the response option, metacognitive error, or simply a tendency to use the higher end of the scale). The operationalization conflates decision confidence with the experiential quality of memory, which is central to the paper's key construct.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace).

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration for any experiment
issues.description: None of the four experiments appear to have been pre-registered. Given the evolving designs across experiments (different response displays, different timing parameters, balanced vs. unbalanced stimulus sets, lab vs. online), the sequential Bayesian stopping rules in Experiments 3-4 (applied to one specific comparison but not others), and the many researcher degrees of freedom in defining exclusion criteria and the 'high confidence' threshold, pre-registration would be important for establishing that the analytic approach was not determined post-hoc.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Stopping rule based on one test among many
issues.description: In Experiments 3 and 4, the sequential Bayesian stopping rule was based on 'the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets.' However, multiple other tests are also reported (main effects, other interactions, follow-up tests). The stopping rule optimizes for one specific comparison while the others are analyzed on the same data without adjustment or acknowledgment that they were not part of the stopping criterion. Additionally, no maximum sample size or stopping rule for null results is mentioned.
issues.quote: Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets.

issues.subcategory: Online data collection without display calibration
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online with participants using their own laptops. There was no control over monitor size, resolution, viewing distance, ambient lighting, or display calibration. Since the task requires discriminating between letters and their mirror-reversed counterparts presented briefly (250 ms) at relatively small sizes, variability in display conditions could systematically affect perceptual encoding quality across participants. This is not discussed as a limitation.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming from letters to visual perception in general
issues.description: The discussion extrapolates from letter/pseudo-letter stimuli to claims about visual memory in general ('memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general' and 'very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input'). Letters are a highly overlearned, categorical stimulus class with strong semantic associations. It is unjustified to generalize these findings to all visual percepts without evidence from other stimulus domains.
issues.quote: it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general. This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.

issues.subcategory: Differential interference timing across delay conditions
issues.description: In Experiments 2-4, the irrelevant second display always appears at 3.75 seconds after memory display offset regardless of condition. In the Long condition (cue at 3s), the second display appears only 0.5s after the cue offset, while in the Short condition (cue at 0.5s), the second display appears 3.0s after the cue. This means the irrelevant display could differentially interfere with post-cue retrieval processes across conditions, confounding the delay manipulation with differential proximity of interference to retrieval.
issues.quote: 3.75 seconds after the offset of the memory display, the second display was presented for 0.25 seconds

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent short delay durations across experiments
issues.description: The short delay condition varies across experiments without acknowledgment: 750 ms in Experiment 1, 500 ms in Experiments 2 and 4. Results are compared across experiments as if these conditions are equivalent, but the 50% difference in delay duration (500 vs 750 ms) could matter given that memory decay is the key variable of interest.
issues.quote: the memory cue appeared after a blank of 0.75 seconds (Short)

issues.subcategory: Possible mischaracterization of Fuzzy Trace Theory
issues.description: The authors claim that FTT predicts high similarity between target and lure should inhibit false memories, and use this to argue FTT cannot account for their findings. However, FTT's prediction about similarity is more nuanced: the distinctiveness heuristic and recollection rejection operate on verbatim traces, but when verbatim traces are weak (as in brief displays), gist-based processing should dominate regardless of similarity. The authors may be applying FTT predictions for recognition paradigms to a visual STM paradigm where they may not straightforwardly apply.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories. This is not consistent with the current data

issues.subcategory: Missing effect sizes and descriptive statistics
issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayes Factors for model comparisons but does not report conventional effect sizes (e.g., η², Cohen's d) for any of the effects. Standard deviations or confidence intervals for the error rate percentages are also not reported, making it impossible to assess the variability of the effects across participants or to compute power for future replications.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay, and a Target Type * Error Type and Memory Delay * Error Type interaction had the best fit (BFm = 18

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous additional exclusion in Experiment 3
issues.description: In Experiment 3, 5 participants were first excluded for having too few high confidence trials. Then it is stated that 'Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.' It is unclear whether this additional participant is one of the 5 already excluded or a 6th exclusion, resulting in ambiguity about the final sample size (58 or 59 in the ANOVA).
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: Training procedure inconsistently applied across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 1 used an extensive training procedure with a 75% correct criterion that excluded 10% of participants, ensuring motivated and proficient participants. Experiments 2-4 did not include this training 'in order to not make the overall time on task too long.' This methodological inconsistency means that the participant populations differ systematically in verified visual memory proficiency across experiments, complicating cross-experiment comparisons.
issues.quote: Since only 10% of participants were excluded based on the training scores, the training procedure was not part of Experiments 2, 3 and 4 in order to not make the overall time on task too long.

issues.subcategory: Response bias alternative not fully ruled out
issues.description: The authors argue against response bias by noting that the pseudo-to-real asymmetry is stronger for high-confidence than low-confidence trials, which they claim is opposite to what response bias predicts. However, this argument assumes response bias operates uniformly across confidence levels. A more sophisticated response bias account could posit that high-confidence responses are precisely those where the familiar category (real letters) is most strongly activated, producing both high confidence AND bias toward selecting the real letter. The argument does not conclusively distinguish memory illusions from confidence-correlated response bias.
issues.quote: if the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias...should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses.

issues.subcategory: Gender reporting inconsistency
issues.description: Demographics are reported inconsistently across experiments: Experiments 1-3 report the number of female participants, while Experiment 4 reports the number of male participants, making comparison across experiments needlessly difficult.
issues.quote: 95 participants participated (28 men; age range 17-41 years, average age 20.8 years)

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 cannot test temporal hypothesis
issues.description: Experiment 3 only includes the Long (3-second) delay condition, making it unable to test Hypothesis 2 (that illusions increase as memory deteriorates over time). While the authors acknowledge this, presenting Experiment 3 as one of four experiments that 'consistently show' STM illusions may overstate the contribution, as it provides no evidence for the temporal dynamics that are central to distinguishing memory from perceptual illusions.
issues.quote: However, Experiment 3 did not test whether expectancy induced memory illusions also increased over time, as the memory trace for the memory display declined.
